Rush
rŭsh
n. and v. (a marsh reed, the lowliest growth of the water; also to move with violence, as nations rushing)
Old English risce, a reed of wet ground; and separately, Middle English ruschen, to move violently. The Authorized Version carries both, and Isaiah plays on the first as a figure of the meanest man in Israel.

Biblical Definition

Bildad opens with a question about the plant: “Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?” (Job 8:11) — the rush is the reed of the marsh, green while the water lasts and withered the moment it fails, and Bildad uses it (wrongly, as applied to Job) as a figure of the hypocrite's hope. Isaiah takes the same plant as the bottom of a society: “Therefore the LORD will cut off from Israel head and tail, branch and rush, in one day” (Isa 9:14), and of Egypt, “Neither shall there be any work for Egypt, which the head or tail, branch or rush, may do” (Isa 19:15). Judgment removes the great and the small together; nobody is beneath it. The verb carries the other sense and one of Isaiah's grandest images: “The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but God shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind” (Isa 17:13). The noise of nations is immense and it is answered by a rebuke.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives rush as a plant of the genus Juncus, growing in wet ground, and proverbially a thing of no value; and to rush as to move forward with impetuosity, violence and tumultuous rapidity.

expand to see more

RUSH, n. A plant growing in wet land, of the genus Juncus. Rushes were formerly used for strewing floors.

2. Proverbially, a thing of small value or importance.

RUSH, v.i. To move forward with impetuosity, violence and tumultuous rapidity.

The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters. Isa. xvii.

Key Scripture

Job 8:11 — "Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?"

Isa 9:14 — "Therefore the LORD will cut off from Israel head and tail, branch and rush, in one day."

Isa 17:13 — "The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but God shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind."

Isa 19:15 — "Neither shall there be any work for Egypt, which the head or tail, branch or rush, may do."

Modern Corruption

The roar of the nations is mistaken for the decisive power in history, when Isaiah answers the rushing of many waters with a single rebuke.

expand to see more

Isaiah 17:13 is built to be heard as well as read. The first half is enormous — nations rushing like the rushing of many waters, a sound that fills the world and admits no argument. The second half is one clause: but God shall rebuke them. What follows is not a battle but a scattering; chaff on a mountain before the wind, and a rolling thing before the whirlwind. The corruption to name is the settled modern assumption, shared by the anxious and the triumphant alike, that the loud thing is the real thing. Whole Christian ministries now organise themselves around the noise of the nations, either in dread of it or in the hope of steering it, and the effect in both cases is that the church takes its agenda from the roar. The prophet gives the roar one verse and the rebuke half of one, and the proportion is deliberate.

The plant half of the word is Isaiah's other lesson and it cuts the opposite way. When the LORD cuts off head and tail, branch and rush, the reed is named alongside the palm branch; the mean and the mighty go in one day. This is a standing refutation of the idea that judgment falls on the powerful while the ordinary man is a bystander. It also guards against the reverse sentimentality, common in our own preaching, which treats the poor as innocent by definition. Scripture is tender toward the poor and fierce against those who oppress them, and it never says that being small is being righteous. Bildad's question about the rush is true in itself, however unjustly he aimed it: a reed with no water withers while it is yet green, and any life not rooted in God is exactly that green and exactly that brief.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gome (H1573), the papyrus rush of the marshes; agmon (H100), a reed or bulrush, the humble growth of Isaiah's pairs; shaah (H7582), to rush or roar, of the nations.

expand to see more

Hebrew gome (H1573) — papyrus, bulrush; the ark of bulrushes in which Moses was laid; Exodus 2:3, Job 8:11.

Hebrew agmon (H100) — a rush, a reed; branch and rush, the top and bottom of a people; Isaiah 9:14, Isaiah 19:15.

Hebrew shaah (H7582) — to make a rushing noise, to roar; the nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters; Isaiah 17:13.

Hebrew gaar (H1605) — to rebuke; the single word that scatters them; Isaiah 17:13, Psalm 106:9.

Hebrew mots (H4671) — chaff; what the nations become when rebuked; Isaiah 17:13, Psalm 1:4.

Usage

"“Can the rush grow up without mire?” — green while the water lasts."

"“Head and tail, branch and rush, in one day” — the great and the small together."

"“But God shall rebuke them” — one clause against the roar of nations."
